newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Media clampdown in Serbia ahead of key elections.
newsitem.headline: Media clampdown in Serbia ahead of key elections.

text.p: Yugoslav authorities have closed 55 local radio and television stations in Serbia this year in a clampdown on independent media ahead of crucial elections, an independent media group said on Wednesday.
The Association of Independent Electronic Media (ANEM), five of whose 25 members were affected by the crackdown, said this was the biggest action against electronic media in Yugoslavia.
Media control is vital to the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) ahead of the autumn presidential elections, scheduled for September 21.
The vote will pick a successor to Slobodan Milosevic, the Socialist strongman sworn in as Yugoslav federal president on Wednesday after ruling Serbia for a decade.
Freedom of the press figured prominently in the platform of huge protests by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition across Serbia last winter which seriously challenged Milosevic's rule.
Zajedno won local elections last November in Serbia's 14 biggest towns, including the Yugoslav capital Belgrade.
The West has repeatedly warned Serbian authorities against cracking down on independent media which are indispensable to any broad public airing of opposition views.

The opposition says state-run television, the basic disseminator of information to a population too poor to buy newspapers regularly, has a heavy pro-SPS bias. There are a handful of independent newspapers and electronic media outlets but their reach is limited mainly to a few larger towns.

The United States says a key condition for improved relations between Washington and Belgrade -- which would help end international financial sanctions against Yugoslavia -- depends on better press freedoms in Serbia.
Serbian authorities argue that many private broadcasters do not have an operating licence.

But ANEM said the Yugoslav telecommunications ministry has not given any indications how and when it would begin issuing "temporary licenses pending adoption of new regulations", as it had announced earlier.
Most of the 55 stations were small local ones, including ANEM members TV Trstenik, TV Pancevo, Radio Boom 93, Radio OK Studio and Radio Pozega.
ANEM appealed on radio and TV stations to provide broadcasting time for those that have been shut down.
"We have started re-broadcasting four hours of news programme by satellite for our members," an editor at independent B92 radio told Reuters.

Milosevic accused a large part of Yugoslav media of being destructive. "A lot of the media is in the service of spiritual and especially moral destruction and is often financially, politically and morally supported from abroad," he said.
